figures.title: The Trace Mineral Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Nine minerals needed in amounts under 20 mg a day.

segments.name: Trace Minerals
segments.text: The last micronutrient lesson covers the trace minerals: nine elements you need in amounts under about twenty milligrams a day, some only in micrograms.

segments.name: Four Groups
segments.text: They're grouped by job. Iron and copper for blood and oxygen; zinc and selenium for enzymes and defense; iodine for the thyroid; and fluoride, manganese, chromium and molybdenum for teeth, bones and enzymes.
segments.cue: The second and third rows, left to right

segments.name: Too Little
segments.text: The bottom row shows what happens with too little. Iron deficiency causes anemia, and iodine deficiency causes goiter. Several others are rarely short in a varied diet. Each box links to its figure.

segments.name: Small Amounts, Big Jobs
segments.text: Most trace minerals sit at the active center of enzymes or other proteins, so tiny amounts matter.

segments.name: A Narrow Window
segments.text: For several of them, especially iron, selenium and fluoride, the gap between enough and too much is small, so food is safer than high-dose supplements. And soil and the rest of the meal affect how much you get.

figures.title: Iron and Heme
figures.subtitle: Two charges, and iron held in a ring.

segments.name: Two Charges
segments.text: Iron is carried as an ion with either two or three positive charges: ferrous iron and ferric iron. It switches between them by gaining or losing one electron.

segments.name: Useful but Risky
segments.text: That easy switching is what makes iron useful for carrying oxygen and electrons. It's also why loose iron can spark damaging reactions, so your body keeps it bound to proteins.

segments.name: Heme
segments.text: Here's heme. An iron atom sits at the center, held by four nitrogens of a large flat ring made of four smaller rings: a porphyrin ring.

segments.name: Oxygen Binds Here
segments.text: In hemoglobin, heme sits in a pocket of the protein, and oxygen binds to the iron from above. The two acid side chains help hold it in place.

segments.name: Heme and Nonheme
segments.text: Heme iron comes only from meat, poultry and fish, and it's absorbed well. Nonheme iron, the form in plants, eggs, dairy and fortified foods, is absorbed less well and depends on the rest of the meal.

segments.name: Absorption
segments.text: Iron is absorbed in the upper small intestine. Heme iron is taken up whole. Nonheme iron must first be changed from ferric to ferrous iron, and vitamin C helps with that.

segments.name: Transport and Use
segments.text: In blood, iron travels bound to a protein called transferrin. About seventy percent of your iron is in hemoglobin in red blood cells and myoglobin in muscle.

segments.name: Storage and Recycling
segments.text: Spare iron is stored as ferritin in the liver, spleen and bone marrow. Old red cells are broken down and their iron reused. Your body has no active way to get rid of extra iron, so it controls how much it absorbs.

segments.name: Iron Facts
segments.text: Men and women over fifty need eight milligrams a day; women nineteen to fifty need eighteen, to replace menstrual losses, and twenty-seven in pregnancy. Iron deficiency is the most common nutrient deficiency in the world, causing tiredness and anemia.

segments.name: Too Much
segments.text: The upper limit is forty-five milligrams a day. Iron supplements are dangerous for young children, so keep them out of reach. Good sources are red meat, shellfish, sardines, lentils, beans, tofu and pumpkin seeds.

figures.title: Zinc and Copper
figures.subtitle: Enzyme metals that compete with each other.

segments.name: Zinc
segments.text: Zinc gives up two electrons and never changes charge. It holds proteins in shape, including zinc fingers that grip DNA, and it's the working part of about a hundred enzymes.

segments.name: Zinc Facts
segments.text: It's needed for immunity, wound healing, growth, and taste and smell. Men need eleven milligrams a day, women eight. Oysters are by far the richest source, then beef, crab, pumpkin seeds and beans.

segments.name: Copper
segments.text: Copper, like iron, switches between two charges, so it works in enzymes that move electrons. It's needed to make energy and connective tissue, and to move iron out of storage, so a shortage can cause anemia.

segments.name: Copper Facts
segments.text: Adults need nine hundred micrograms a day, from oysters, liver, nuts, seeds, mushrooms and dark chocolate. Deficiency is rare.

segments.name: They Compete
segments.text: Zinc and copper compete for absorption. Long-term high-dose zinc supplements can cause copper deficiency.

segments.name: Selenocysteine
segments.text: Selenium sits just below sulfur in the periodic table. Swap the sulfur in cysteine for selenium and you get selenocysteine, sometimes called the twenty-first amino acid. It's built into about twenty-five human proteins.

segments.name: In Plants
segments.text: Plants take up selenium from soil and build it into selenomethionine, in place of methionine. So the selenium in plant foods depends on where they grew.

segments.name: What It Does
segments.text: Selenium proteins include antioxidant enzymes and the enzymes that activate thyroid hormone. Adults need fifty-five micrograms a day. Deficiency is rare in the US.

segments.name: Brazil Nuts
segments.text: Too much causes selenosis: garlic breath, brittle hair and nails. A single Brazil nut can contain more than a day's needs, so eat them only occasionally. Fish, eggs, poultry and whole grains are steady sources.

segments.name: Iodide
segments.text: Iodine is taken in as iodide, a large negative ion. Your thyroid gland traps it from the blood.

segments.name: Thyroxine
segments.text: The thyroid builds iodide into thyroxine: two rings joined by an oxygen, with two iodines on each ring. Four iodines, so it's called T4. It's built from the amino acid tyrosine.

segments.name: T3
segments.text: In body tissues a selenium enzyme removes one outer iodine, giving T3, the active hormone. Thyroid hormones set your metabolic rate and are essential for brain development before birth and in infancy.

segments.name: Iodine Facts
segments.text: Adults need a hundred and fifty micrograms a day, two hundred and twenty in pregnancy. Too little causes goiter, an enlarged thyroid, and in pregnancy can impair the baby's brain development. Seaweed, fish, dairy, eggs and iodized salt are the main sources.

segments.name: Not All Salt
segments.text: Sea salt, kosher salt and most salt in processed foods usually aren't iodized.

segments.name: Four Ions
segments.text: Here are the last four, as the ions or compound they're carried in. Molybdenum arrives mostly as molybdate, a molybdenum atom with four oxygens.

segments.name: Fluoride
segments.text: Fluoride replaces the OH in tooth enamel, making it more resistant to acid. Too little means more tooth decay; too much while teeth are forming causes white flecks. Fluoridated water and tea are the main sources.

segments.name: Manganese and Chromium
segments.text: Manganese is part of enzymes for bone and metabolism, and an antioxidant enzyme. Chromium may help insulin work, though supplements show little clear benefit. Shortage of either is rare.

segments.name: Molybdenum
segments.text: Molybdenum is a cofactor for four enzymes. Beans, lentils and whole grains supply plenty, and deficiency in healthy people is essentially unknown.

figures.title: Absorption and Labels
figures.subtitle: What helps and blocks absorption, and Daily Values.

segments.name: Helpers and Blockers
segments.text: What else is in the meal matters. Vitamin C and meat increase nonheme iron absorption. Phytate in whole grains and beans lowers iron and zinc absorption, and tea and coffee lower iron absorption.

segments.name: Easier to Absorb
segments.text: Soaking beans, sprouting grains and fermenting bread break down phytate. And cooking acidic foods in a cast-iron pan adds some iron.

segments.name: Daily Values
segments.text: The Daily Values are listed in this table: eighteen milligrams of iron, eleven of zinc, a hundred and fifty micrograms of iodine, and so on.

segments.name: On the Label
segments.text: Iron must appear on every Nutrition Facts label. The others appear only if added or claimed.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here are the nine trace minerals in one table: their main job, what happens with too little, and whole-food sources.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Heme, vitamin B12 and chlorophyll all hold a metal in the same kind of ring. Each blood donation removes about two hundred to two hundred and fifty milligrams of iron. And iodized salt, introduced in the US in 1924, all but eliminated goiter. Try the quiz below.
